reference.source: Respiratory Medicine and Thoracic Surgery reference texts
clinicalPearls: Recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax in a menstruating woman occurring around the time of menses (typically within a couple of days before or after onset)
Overwhelmingly right-sided, reflecting the pattern of thoracic endometriosis and diaphragmatic involvement
Part of the thoracic endometriosis syndrome, which also includes catamenial haemothorax, haemoptysis, and lung nodules
Diaphragmatic defects (fenestrations) and endometrial implants on the diaphragm and pleura are frequently found at surgery
Should be suspected in any woman of reproductive age with recurrent or right-sided spontaneous pneumothorax, especially with a history of pelvic endometriosis
Management combines surgical repair of diaphragmatic defects and pleurodesis with hormonal suppression to prevent recurrence
Recurrence is common if the endometriosis is not addressed medically alongside surgical treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Catamenial pneumothorax is closely linked to thoracic endometriosis, in which ectopic endometrial tissue reaches the diaphragm, visceral, and parietal pleura, likely through transdiaphragmatic passage of cells from the peritoneum, retrograde menstruation, or microembolisation. Cyclical hormonal stimulation causes these implants and associated diaphragmatic fenestrations to bleed and slough with menstruation, and defects in the diaphragm may allow peritoneal air to pass into the pleural space. Additional proposed mechanisms include prostaglandin-mediated alveolar rupture. The result is air entering the thorax in temporal relationship with the menstrual cycle, characteristically on the right where diaphragmatic defects predominate.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax from underlying lung disease
Catamenial haemoptysis or haemothorax from thoracic endometriosis
additionalInvestigations: Detailed menstrual and gynaecological history correlating episodes with the cycle
CT of the thorax to assess for diaphragmatic defects, nodules, and cysts
Video-assisted thoracoscopy for direct inspection of the diaphragm and pleura
Histological confirmation of endometrial tissue in resected specimens
Assessment for associated catamenial haemothorax or haemoptysis
redFlags: Tension physiology with haemodynamic compromise requiring emergency decompression
Repeated recurrences despite intervention indicating untreated endometriosis
Large or bilateral pneumothorax causing significant respiratory distress
reference.prognosis: With combined surgical repair, pleurodesis, and hormonal suppression, recurrence can be markedly reduced, but treatment with surgery alone is associated with high recurrence; long-term outlook is generally good once the underlying endometriosis is controlled.
pitfalls: Not linking recurrent right-sided pneumothorax to the menstrual cycle and missing the diagnosis
Treating with pleurodesis alone without hormonal suppression, leading to recurrence
Failing to involve gynaecology in the management of underlying endometriosis
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Acute management of the pneumothorax with observation, aspiration or intercostal chest drain according to size and symptoms
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery to repair diaphragmatic fenestrations and resect endometrial and pleural implants
Pleurodesis, mechanical or chemical, to obliterate the pleural space and reduce recurrence
Hormonal suppression of endometrial tissue with gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonists, given the high recurrence with surgery alone
Combined care with gynaecology to manage coexisting pelvic endometriosis
Surveillance for recurrence and for associated catamenial haemothorax or haemoptysis
Multidisciplinary thoracic surgery and gynaecology input
